reason: The court merely distinguished Girantha because it construed the old section 121, so the proposed rule is overbroad and not supported as a general proposition.
The appeal turned on the plaintiff's failure in a declaration of title action to plead and strictly prove the title asserted.
The court set aside relief because it could not grant a declaration on a case not both pleaded and proved.
The court treated the late new position taken after the defendant had closed his case as impermissible and material to allowing the appeal.
The statement captures the rent-certainty point but drops the Agrarian Services Act and paddy-field context and the court's fuller fixed-or-readily-ascertainable qualification.
The court rejected the Public Trustee or devalagama-land objection and held that paddy fields remained subject to the paddy/agricultural land regime.
The court directly decided that one joint ande cultivator could transfer his rights to the other and that succession did not pass to heirs in that situation.
The result is correct for P22, but the statement is tautological and omits that the existing LRC monthly lease required a legal and proper notice of termination.
The court used this Roman-Dutch-law distinction between personal lease rights and rights in rem to uphold the petitioner's monthly lease status.
The estoppel holding depended materially on the proved leases and the defendants' predecessor accepting the plaintiff's lessor title, which the statement omits.
The court did not say long possession alone can never found ouster, but held that possession must be assessed with income, value, relationship, residence, and the facts of exclusion.
The court expressly limited the partition court's title investigation to the pleadings, admissions, points of contest, and oral and documentary evidence before it.
The failure of the fiscal conveyance claim turned on the court's holding that trust property could not be seized and sold in execution.
The statement reflects the result but omits the material fact that only the alleged right, title, and interest of a trustee with no proved vested share had been transmitted.
The deed proof objection failed because no objection was taken when the documents were read at the close of the plaintiff's case.
The court held the defendants were not bona fide possessors and could not force unsolicited improvements on the owner and claim compensation.
The statement omits the court's express exception where the owner stands by and allows building without notice of his own claim.
The partition-title duty was upheld, but the cited Civil Procedure Code section 146 concerned framing issues and was not the provision actually construing that title-investigation duty.
The court construed section 60 on the basis that the state lending institution's purchaser was to have a quick and effective recovery-of-possession remedy.
The case was about ejecting persons outside section 60(3) and (4) by virtue of the certificate of sale, not about a party failing to comply with certificate requirements.
The statement is too vague and malformed to express any holding, even though the headnote mentions consequential enabling provisions.
The court applied the three stated conditions for fresh evidence under section 773 and refused the application because the documents would not affect the appeal.
The court did not state a general rule that deeds may be considered at a hearing, but refused these deeds because they did not touch the trial issues.
The court used ownership and consequent entitlement to possession as the cause of action in rei vindicatio when rejecting the defective-plaint objection.
The statement omits that the parol evidence must relate to grounds in the proviso to section 92 and does not apply where the deed is only incidentally considered.
